sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Haoma** ​(*haoma*) — ‌Sacred Plant, ‌Immortality ​· The ​pressed one ​— ​belongs to ​the Zoroastrian ‌tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain ‌"Sacred Plant, ​Immortality". The ‌name ​means "The ​pressed one"[^1].

​**Haoma** ​is the ​deified sacred ‌plant ​of Zoroastrianism, ‌pressed at ​the ‌dawn liturgy ​into the ‌draught ​that grants ‌vigor, wisdom, ​and ​a share ‌in immortality. ‌Green and ‌golden-eyed, ​hymned as ​a yazata ‌in ​his own ​right, he ‌is ​the tradition's ​living sacrament ‌— ​god, offering, ‌and medicine ​crushed ​in a ​single mortar ​— ‌and the ‌Iranian double ​of ‌the Vedic ​soma.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records the ‌canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Haoma** and ‌serves ​its temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/haoma/). ​The displayed ​form is ‌ASCII-equivalent ​— a ​description computed ​from ‌the displayed ​form itself. ​The ​plain ASCII ‌form *haoma* ​contains ‌the same ​letters: no ‌recovered diacritics ​or ‌special encoding ‌is claimed. ​The ​work here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested in ​Avestan ​as ​**𐬵𐬀𐬊𐬨𐬀**. ​Etymologically ​it means ‌"The ​pressed ​one"[^1].

‌The ​canonical ‌spelling **Haoma** ​matches ‌the ​conventional ​scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ​ASCII ‌form ​*haoma* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters, ​so ‌no ​lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ​transition ‌is ‌claimed. ‌The ​editorial work ​is ‌to ​fix ​one ‌reviewed reference ​spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and ‌provenance, ​and keep ​the ​original ​evidence ‌visible. ‌The displayed ​form ‌is ​ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a ‌description computed ‌from ‌the ​displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation ‌runs:

- ​**h** ​→ ​**H** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ​**a** ​→ ‌**a** — ​Same
- ‌**o** ​→ ‌**o** ​— ‌Same
- **m** ‌→ ​**m** ​— ​Same
- ​**a** → ‌**a** ‌— ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/haoma/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**haoma** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Haoma.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Haoma" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Haoma" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"haoma" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Haoma ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Haoma ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Haoma ‌place ​sacred plant, ​immortality ​at ​the center ​of ‌a living ​mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Haoma ‌appears ​in zoroastrian ‌tradition ​as sacred ​plant, ​immortality. ​The name's ​meaning, ‌"The ​pressed one", ‌shapes ​the narratives ‌told ​about ‌this figure.

### ​Worship ‌and ​Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ‌and later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved ​Haoma in ​ritual, ‌text, ​and iconography, ​ensuring ‌the name ​survived ​into ‌the modern ​scholarly ‌record.

​The myths ​of ​Haoma survive ​in ‌fragments, ‌summaries, and ​later ‌retellings. ​Each version ​reflects ‌the interests ‌of ‌its ‌tellers — ​poets, ‌priests, ​philosophers, and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does ​not privilege ​a ‌single ​version; it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Haoma ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or artifact ​in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet assigned ​to ‌Haoma ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should be ​read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Zoroastrian ​name ‌of this ​type ‌the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected to ​be ​thin, ‌and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains the ‌textual ​testimony ​gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources section.

​Were ‌such ​evidence ​to ​surface, ​it ‌would take ‌recognizable ​forms: ‌votive ​or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming 𐬵𐬀𐬊𐬨𐬀, ‌sanctuary ‌or ​cult ‌remains ​tied ​to sacred ​plant ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional ​attributes (name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be ‌weighed against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name ​before entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Haoma ​asks ‌what ‌a ​sacrament ​is. ​Not a ​symbol, ​exactly ‌— ​the ​plant ‌is ​eaten; ‌not ​a ‌drug ​alone ​— ​the ethics ​police ​it; ‌not ​a ‌metaphor ​— ‌the ​god ‌answers ​back. ‌The ​rite's deepest ​claim ‌is ‌that ‌matter ​can ​be ‌holy ​without ​ceasing ‌to ​be ​matter: ‌water, twigs, ​milk, ‌prayer, ​a ​mortar, ​a ​morning. ‌In ‌an ​age ‌that ​splits ​body ‌and meaning ‌into ‌separate ‌compartments, ​Haoma's ‌nightly ​chemistry ​lesson ​endures: ‌what ​you ​take ​in shapes ‌what ​you ​are, ​and ‌a ​tradition ‌that ​has ‌blessed ​its ‌breakfast ‌for ​four thousand ​years ​knows ​something ‌about ‌slow ​transformation.[^1]
